utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Could I ask you, please, to read aloud the affirmation on the card that is given to you now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And good afternoon to Their Honours and the Defence team as well as to the witness. The next witness is a protective witness and so I would like to have some assistance by usher here, and in order to provide the witness a piece -- a sheet of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And I would like the witness not to read out loud while we are not in private session what says on the paper. So not -- and I would like the witness to read it through, the information about the witness's particulars, both regard to the date of birth and location of birth and name, and to confirm or not to confirm if it's the -- if the information is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I start to do the examination-in-chief I would like to -- just to give somehow information to the Court concerning this witness. The witness has protective measures, as we all know, and that is face and voice distortion as well as a pseudonym and that is number P16. However, this witness's profession could have the consequences that I would like to ask for private sessions in a more wide, broad manner than I could perhaps do in -- in terms of another sort of witness. Concerning the profession the witness has at the time of the time frame of the indictment, there were only another 15 persons occupying the same profession, and that's why some of the information the witness can -- will give to us could reveal the identification of the witness. I just want to give that kind of information before we start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to start with private session because I would like the witness to describe the witness's professional background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: At the time when you were (redacted) (redacted), can you describe for us in general what kind of areas you did cover? (redacted) And if you know when you're answering the questions so give us a hint so to say so we can go into private session if that is needed, if you think your answer will reveal your identity, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Madam, you said this was something that is quite peculiar. Your Honours, I believe my position was in fact so peculiar that I would be very easy to identify every time I mention names or specific events. There is always a possibility that someone might link these names and events to my identity. I can only offer my apologies, although that is certainly not my fault. I would like to share whatever information I have with you at the expense of the public being informed unfortunately. I will try to answer the question, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have any kind of specialty?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And now we can go into private session if you did have a kind of specialty that could be linked to your identity. So I request for a private session before the witness is answering that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I'm trying to think of something specific because there were always things going on. I'm not sure what might be especially note worthy, if you could please elaborate or tell me what exactly you want me to talk about, then perhaps I can answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get that because I was talking to my case manager. Do you want to go into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is whether you see relevance to going into detail of the work he did in Knin. On the face of it, it is not relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: From the Prosecution side it could be relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Because the -- depends on the answer from the witness, of course, but there are -- if the witness will mention a specific name of a certain fighter, and that will have relevance for the case later on, in terms of the individual criminal responsibility for one of the Accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this an issue of identification or of conduct of that person at Knin?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: It's more about the conduct of the person in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How is that relevant to what happened at Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In Knin, if the -- I can't say what the witness perhaps will tell us here, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But if the witness did certain things in Knin --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- how does that prove that he did some other thing or the same thing in Vukovar, if that's what you're getting at?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'm getting at if now the witness answers in a certain specific way, that the witness perhaps would mention a name of a certain fighter that was present at a certain occasion in Vukovar for the time frame of our indictment. And that is in terms of the behaviour of that person in Knin that the witness encountered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Now I would like to move over to Vukovar. And I would like to ask the witness when the witness were present in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Now there is a problem here again. This is very important, and I'm going to start naming names. So for me to be able to give valid answers to your questions, we have to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request for private session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have reached the time when the tapes must be rewound so we will adjourn. As there have been redactions, we must adjourn for half an hour. Now, Mrs. Tuma, there have been some markings on a map. Are you wanting those preserved?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. Yes, I do want to have that and we can, before we end this session, I would like to admit that as an evidence and exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It stops at Negoslavci. Is that what you want?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The witness had marked here from Sid up until entering of Vukovar. So that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well, yes. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 111, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We now adjourn and will resume at quarter past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Are we still in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No. You want to go back to private?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would request private session, please, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like now to go to use another map that has been used in this case, and that is Exhibit number 48, number 48, with the ERN number 04639058. Thank you. Does the witness have the sketch plan in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I do have the sketch in front of me, but it's quite pale and very small.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We'll see if you can get some assistance here, if it's possible to make it clearer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Can we zoom out a little? It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay. So when you reached the hospital, where did you go? And can you please mark that on the sketch, please? And you can have the number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour, for reacting this soon. In my submission, this sketch was produced by one of the witnesses in this trial and this is an especially leading question by the OTP. There are handwritten markings made by that witness on the map, which indicates to the witness what he's expected to say. I believe this is essentially of a leading nature, the entire exercise. We should have given him a blank one, have him draw it and then mark it himself. I believe I'm right in suggesting this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Borovic, that the general layout of the hospital is one that has not been sufficiently contentious for this witness to indicate where it was he was. As far as I know, but you may be proved right, but as far as I know, he has not going to give us a detailed description of everything that was in the hospital. He is merely going to indicate where he was, and I think that can be done on this map. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So can the witness please mark with a number -- figure 1, where you went when you came to the hospital? And tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: As I've already said, I turned off the main street, what I believe to be the main street at the time, down the gentle slope and within a matter of minutes I was standing in front of the annex which I believe is the new part of the hospital. This was the only part of the hospital that I saw. I arrived right there in front. The road was relatively broad. It was an asphalt road. There were steps in front, and the facade was made of glass, as far as I remember. There were two glass doors. There was an extension - I'm not sure how long the extension was - in front of the hospital, how long the asphalt road was. There were ambulances parked there. So that was the first image that I caught sight of when I reached this entrance to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I see a red marking. What will that show? Can the witness explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: The red marking shows the spot where I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. And when you were standing there, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: The first thing I saw to my left was a pile of dirty bandages. That was the first thing I set eyes on within my sight. To the right there was a small chair or rather a small table, there was a bin liner on the table and protruding from the bin liner was a bit of a lower arm belonging to a man. It was placed against the wall. This was the first photograph that I took in Vukovar, and I took maybe two or three shots of this, moving left and right, looking for a perfect angle.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. I will return back to the cross that you made on this sketch. I asked you to number it with number 1 as well. So please put -- please do that, where you were standing and make the marking, number 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And I would like to admit that into evidence as an exhibit, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are there any other markings you want on this? Or is that the marking?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Depends on the witness's answer but probably that could be another -- number 2 marking, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, if you move quickly, we might get it on to this exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: With due respect, I would like to keep the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not convenient? Very well. We will receive this now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit 112, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When were you standing there, can you in your memory say -- tell us what time of the day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: It was in the early afternoon hours. It was a lovely day, really, sunny. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: (redacted) So in answer to your question, early afternoon hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were standing there, did you speak to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Well, I was focused on that arm. When I raised my eyes I saw the hospital entrance, and standing between the two doors I saw two tall police officers. Just across the way I saw a captain whom I had not seen on my way there. He was leaning against the wall, hands behind his back.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I have what you might term a photographic memory. I'm lucky to have it, I should say. That was at least what they told me when we were tested once back at school. I have a great memory for landscapes, faces, images. I'm not that good with numbers and names, though. But if I see someone, a person, two or three times, I tend to memorise them, and the person I recognised there was Captain Radic. Usually you remember the person's first name or last name, or the nickname, and the only bit that I remembered about this person was his last name, Radic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Have you been -- have you been seeing him before, in any context?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And now we can go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you were standing there and you saw Captain Radic, did you see anything else when you were standing there? And please tell us that, what you saw. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: At this time, I saw military policemen opening the door, and I saw soldiers bringing out who I believed were Croatian prisoners of war on

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: taking them to camouflaged JNA ambulances.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Could you estimate how many you saw at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I spent about 15 minutes there, and I can say with certainty that between 15 and 20 different persons were carried off on stretchers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: In what way were those persons laying on the stretchers dressed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: What really stunned me at the time, based at least on the images that I saw around me in Vukovar, that was the only rational sight that I could behold in Vukovar at the time. They were clean-shaven, their pajamas were clean. They were light blue with stripes. They looked very neat, to me, as though this wasn't war and as though it wasn't Vukovar. So that's the one image that I remember. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: (redacted) Some of them had visible injuries. I saw their arms and legs bandaged, while some others had no injuries that could be readily seen. Some of them were not even prone on the stretcher. They were sort of sitting on stretchers. At least those 15 to 20 that I saw were young men, young and good-looking, aged for the most part between 20 and 30. I don't think there was a single one among them that was aged over 25. They were really quite young.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. So you spent 15 minutes there and you were standing there. Did you have a conversation with anyone at that time? And who was that, in that case?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: (redacted) I greeted Captain Radic but he cut me dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What -- was there anything more said at this time? And I would like to remind the witness that we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I found it strange and it was an unpleasant feeling. You know the feeling when you greet someone and the person doesn't greet you back. He was looking straight ahead of him. I was trying to save the day so I asked him how many wounded there were, just like that, for no particular reason. I wasn't even interested in the number at the time. Yet there was no reply from him. And I started muttering to myself but out loud saying something like this: "It's good that there should be as many as possible so we can exchange them for those of our soldiers who had been captured." He was looking at the wounded who were being carried off, and he asked me, "Do you know how many of our men they killed?" This was easier for me now so I simply replied by saying, "I have no idea, no one is writing about it. No one is talking about it." We stood there looking at the wounded people being stretchered off. I remarked for no special reason, "Look at them, how nice-looking and clean shaven they are." I said it for nothing, just like that, because that was the only rational thing I was able to behold around me at the time. And he replied, "These are dead men." My reaction was a knee-jerk reaction, as it were. I said, "But these people are alive." And he told me, "No, you can't see right. These people are dead." I really felt very uncomfortable. It had already become a routine for me to have all these experiences of various kinds in the war. I took two steps in the direction of the hospital and I was talking to myself, I said aloud, "Off I go to do some work." It was a kind of defence mechanism, a reaction. I wanted to be rid of that uncomfortable situation. As I approached the hospital down at the far end of the corridor I spotted Major Sljivancanin and I told myself, "This is really not your lucky day. I'll try not to meet this one." Then I turned back and walked back the same way that I had walked to reach the hospital in the first place. The reason I decided not to enter was because I had seen Sljivancanin there. Why? Allow me to clarify. The previous evening he had put on a show with the International Red Cross representative. To say the least I had found the whole experience sickening. I still remember a lot of what was said, although it has been a long time. He tried to familiarise this person with our history, with our difficulties, telling him something like, "What are you doing here to begin with? Why don't you leave this war to us to wage this war the way we want?" But this was okay within a more collective frame of reference that we used, and most of my colleagues, needless to say, reacted in a negative way. They thought he shouldn't have been explaining all these things to this person, to begin with. I'm not sure what the English expression is but they said stuff like, well, he could go on and on like that until the cows come home. So that was the sort of scene that I witnessed. That was the prefer occasion that I saw him. And particularly this very unpleasant occasion when he was talking to this International Red Cross person. If we go back into private session, maybe I can provide another piece of information just to complete the picture. Briefly, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to go back before we are doing that, to go back with a few questions to ask the witness about this incident. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You mentioned that -- and now we are in open session. You mentioned that you felt uncomfortable when you heard that -- when Captain Radic said that these men are dead. Can you explain that feeling for us? You said you felt uncomfortable. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I'm trying to be rational about this. If you see them at a distance of two metres, young men aged between 20 and 25, and then somebody comes up to you and tells you that these people are dead, well, to say the least it must cause you to feel strange. You start doubting the rational powers of the person you're talking to. You start asking yourself questions, what is this about? I was in no position to go that far. I wasn't considering the possibility but I must say the situation was unpleasant to say the least. Even with all my experience from the war, even with my being used to these situations, but sometimes you have this red alert feeling suddenly out of nowhere and you ask yourself questions, like, is this person sane? That's at least the way I felt at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you go after the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: After the hospital, I walked back the same way. An incident happened that I could perhaps -- that I could clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you would just pause. Thank you. Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I really must offer my apologies but maybe I wasn't clear enough at the outset when I explained this. I think it might be more helpful for someone who is testifying for the first time to be shown a photograph, a blank photograph, so he could use it to indicate where he went and what route he took. If we keep using this sketch, he can read the names of all the rooms that he had perhaps gone to. I move that we adopt a more objective method to further pursue this exercise, at least as far as indicating locations in and around the hospital is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, I would like you, with the witness, first of all to ask him to describe where he went. It may then be useful to get him to indicate on a plan or a map. Whether or not there will be the difficulty that Mr. Borovic foresees will, I think, largely depend on the description first given by the witness. So we will hear that first and then see whether or not there is need to turn to a plan, and if so, what that plan should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So can the witness, without any kind of marking, describe where the witness went after the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: After -- well, I didn't enter the hospital, as I said. So after the hospital, I took the same route. I hadn't gone even five or six metres from the corner of the hospital when two young women passed me by, one had dark hair, the other had brown hair. I turned around and saw that they were wearing white uniforms under their coats. They were 22 or 3 years old. Judging by their coats and the fact that they were young, I assume they were nurses. They went right past me and the dark-haired girl was crying. The one with the lighter hair had her arm over her shoulder and I heard the dark-haired woman say, "How can they say that we are all Ustashas?" And she continued crying and they went off and took the route I had just taken. There was a small wall -- well, a wall of about three metres high, since the annex building was dug into the ground. I saw a gentleman from the International Red Cross whom I recognised because the man on the previous two or three evenings, at least according to the television -- I don't know how much time actually went by, but anyway, he had a heated debate with Major Sljivancanin, and he was standing stock still and looking towards the hospital. There was a vehicle nearby, I think it was a jeep, a Toyota probably, with the International Red Cross emblems and it said Geneva on it and the man was dressed in white with the same International Red Cross, Geneva, insignia. That's what I saw as I was leaving the entrance to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see any other Red Cross personnel at this spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Well, as far as I remember, there might have been a man in a vehicle, but there was just this man standing outside the vehicle, the one I identified from having seen him on television.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. And what did you do next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I set off towards the street, the main road, and I saw a group of photo-reporters, and I went a little further down where there was a park, and I came across a shocking image. There were bodies lined up, lines of bodies, and I thought there were about 80 bodies and I was just wrong on the body count because there were 83 bodies in actual fact, and they were covered with transparent foil. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: (redacted) There were women, men, naked, luckily there weren't any children. But the whole scene was very disturbing and terrible to behold. I can take many things but to see that many bodies in one place is difficult for anybody.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you get any information where these bodies came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was interested in knowing because I saw that their injuries were not caused by bullets. I had grown accustomed to sights like that. There were more civilians there than soldiers, and I asked who the people lying there in the park were, and a woman told me that they were people who had died from the hospital and were brought there because they weren't able to bury them. That's the information I was given. That is to say people who had died a natural death or succumbed to various injuries but because of the war and wartime conditions they weren't able to be buried in the usual manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe anything else on the main street or along the main street?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: eyes -- your eye becomes tired and has to -- you have to have a rest. And then I saw that from the side streets and from all over, that civilians were coming in. So -- and although the weather was very hot, too hot for that time of year, I saw people wearing two coats, for example, they were dirty, you could tell by their hair that they hadn't washed for months. They looked unkempt. And there was a stench, an indefinable stench. I even saw a woman with a baby, (redacted) (redacted), I went up to the woman, she was young, 20-odd years, 22 or 3 maybe, and she told me that the baby was born in a cellar and the baby was 10 days old (redacted). I took down here particulars, the unfortunate woman was crying, the baby was very sweet, just like any other baby. But the other people weren't about to talk to me. They were all very distressed. I remember an old woman. She sat facing the sun and her face resembled parchment and she said, "Leave me alone, my son. I want to get a little heat from the sun after having spent three months in a cellar." And I didn't wish to intrude, and ask them any questions and disturb them. Many of the people were crying. They were in a very poor state and didn't wish to communicate in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. What else did you observe when you were walking along the main street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Well, I set off down that street and then once again we go back to the irrational. Somebody told us to walk in the middle of the street because of the mines, and I knew that even without having to be cautioned. But then you saw you weren't able to take the middle of the street because there were soldiers from different units, driving vehicles without any number plates, driving motorcycles. I saw a car, for instance, which was riddled with about a thousand bullets. It was all bullet-ridden. Every centimetre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Maybe other people wouldn't have noticed things like that but as I say as I was walking up the street I happened to notice a column of buses and they had JNA signs on them, and I even recognised one of the drivers. I think that we -- well, whether he gave me a cigarette or not, that's not important but we knew each other from before and I asked him, "What are you doing here?" And he said, "Well, we've come to evacuate the population." And I continued along my way down the street and I must say I'd never been to Vukovar before that but I recognised the workers' centre from some photographs I had seen. It's a building where the congress was held. So it's a well-known building and easily recognisable. And at that point I saw something that looked like a building. I didn't know at the time whether it was the Dunav hotel. Some youngsters told me that that used to be the building used to be the Danube or Dunav hotel. (redacted) (redacted), a young man came up to me with a beard (redacted) And we had express orders, or, rather, we were told that if we see any people with beards, that we should do everything they asked us to do, that we should be flexible (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to interrupt the witness and continue when the witness were in Vukovar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: You said that you protected. In what way did you -- what did you do in order to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Well, quite simply I stood between the barrel of the gun, my face turned towards the soldier, and the journalist was actually behind me. So I faced the soldier with the gun pointed at me. That was the simplest reaction. I didn't think he would actually shoot at me, although. When I thought about the situation later on, it was risky business because many of them were carrying bottles of alcohol or they were tipsy themselves, and trigger happy. But I was lucky. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: We'll now move over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, we have run out of time.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We have reached the time where we must have another break. There have been redactions so we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And then I would like to request for private session because we will continue with this photograph and that could reveal the identity of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And what happened next after you saw Sljivancanin? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: My colleagues had arrived in the meantime, and one of them said, "We have our subject matter and we have an interesting topic to tackle." He had received information somewhere at the other end of town that there was an evacuation of Vukovar civilians in the offing and that they would all be taken to the reception centre. I sat down with them. I can't describe the route we took, but we reached the far end of town. We arrived at a plateau with low-lying shacks on it or huts. The first definition that occurred to me when I saw this place was some sort of a hauling company. It was a huge area with a parking lot.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: At this plateau, which was rectangular, roughly speaking, the side facing the town, there were about 20 tables there. Seated at these tables were officers, junior officers, soldiers. Each table had a writing on it saying, "Reception centre. Ruma, Sremska Mitrovica," and all these place names. These are some that I remember. Columns formed there and people's names were recorded on a list. They were given canned food and bread, following which they were herded on to buses. But since there were lots of people, they used lorries too. (redacted) we did not talk to those people who were there. There was no need for us to talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did you see anything spectacular at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Nothing spectacular, really, it's only once the plateau had emptied, once the whole scene had been cleared to a large extent, it was across the way that I saw a group comprising about 100 or 200 people standing there. Dusk was approaching. I crossed the street. There was a warehouse for wood and coal. There was a group of people standing there under the eaves. A middle-aged lady came up to me and said, "We are Croats." She grabbed my hand and I could feel her shivering or trembling, and she asked, "What will become of us, mister?" This is the first time that I felt that someone's legs, not just the arms, but someone's legs were shaking. I had the feeling that her foot would come out of that light summer shoe. I tried to soothe her by saying, "There is no problem at all. Once they are done with the Serbs, you will be the next in line to be evacuated." I just said that to calm her, to soothe her, because I had no idea what would actually happen to those people. So there was this group comprising about 150 or 200 people. There were only women, children, and a few elderly men, but not more than six or seven, I reckoned. All in that group were women and children, aged up to 15 for the most part. At this point in time, a military lorry drove up and disgorged about 15 boxes of dry rations, the sort that are used in wartime, the regulation JNA rations for troops on the ground. However, only children went to get those. None of the elderly there were in the mood to go and fetch them. It was only children who went for them. They looked at the cans, they looked at the toast, and as I was talking to that lady, I saw a non-commissioned officer approach me, not sure if he was a corporal or first class corporal. He came up to me and said, "There is nothing for you here. You may as well cross to the other side." Needless to say, I obeyed his instructions. I crossed to the other side, and it was already getting dark and we were getting ready to drive back to Sid. I have no idea what became of those people. I don't know if they were evacuated and how or where they eventually ended up. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you spend the night until the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: It was difficult to get through. We had to drive around this long column made up of buses. We reached Sid late at night and that's where we spent the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the next day, where did you go? What did you do then? Now we are on -- the next day will be on the 19th November.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: My apologies, are we still in closed session?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Now I'm about to name specific names and I think it would probably be a good idea to go back into closed session briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Request for private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'd remind you the issue is whether the names could lead to identification of the witness, but we will proceed on that assumption.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of the transcript, page 59, line 2, I believe the witness said "press centre." This is not reflected in the transcript. So that's the only thing I wish to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Colleagues went to Belgrade and he went to the press centre is my note. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can you describe what you were doing later on? You had a vehicle. Did you get to receive that? And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: As I've just said, this colleague of mine drove up in a vehicle and he had a driver. I joined them and we took the shortest route that was open in order to get to Borovo Naselje. As far as I was familiar with the local geography, Borovo Naselje was a place with lots of industry, factories such as Vutex and Borovo, the well-known factories. We wanted to go there and see what the situation was in this new part of Vukovar. We managed to negotiate this route and smoothly reach Borovo Naselje. Of course, Borovo Naselje too was scarred by war. What I found noteworthy, to the best of my recollection, this is the day after the fall of Vukovar, we saw buildings on fire. We saw tall buildings ablaze, a building with 20 floors was burning from the 15th floor up. We were wondering how was it possible one day after the end of fighting for buildings to still be ablaze. We were told that this now was the paramilitary units going around looting and torching buildings. We were on our way to the centre and you could see these tall buildings from miles away. We came across this one street that I later identified as Vinogradska street. There was some sort of a hedge there and some holes were dug near it. We saw people in those holes wearing gas masks and rain coats. When we came closer we realised there was a row of nice family houses there. We realised that these people were carrying bodies, dead bodies, and dropping them into these holes. I went up and asked them why they were doing this, and they said they were doing this in order to prevent an infection from spreading. This is where my colleague and I parted ways. I entered a house that was new and quite lovely. As soon as I passed the gate, I saw a scene that remains carved in my memory. I assumed those were a mother and a son. The old lady was about 80 years old. She had silver hair. And her son probably wanted to protect her so they were both lying there as if embracing each other - they were mowed down on the spot - and her head was resting against the son's lower arm. They were lying on the floor, both dead, in an embrace. A little further off was another woman, dead, aged about 30, and what really shattered me was a child that I saw lying there near a cellar or a garage. The child must have been aged three or four. Its hair was on its ends, as if somebody had done a special hair-do using a gel. It was from all the rain and the dust. There was a bullet hole in the child's forehead. Whenever I remember this I'm quite crest fallen. I'm used to seeing death. You do as you get older. But one thing I'll never understand is how someone can kill a child. There were more dead in that street. None of them killed by shrapnel. I had a clear view so I can tell. I even quarrelled with one of the undertakers or whatever they were, those people who were carrying the bodies off. He picked up a lady's body and the skirt she had on got snagged on something, so I asked him to be a bit more careful but he was very brusque. He turned back and said, "Well, if you want to do this, please go ahead and take my place." As I say, what I found particularly depressing is that scene with the child. I can forget about all the grownups whose dead bodies I saw but one thing I can never forget is the child. I can't accept the fact that there are human beings around who are capable of killing a child. Once we move on and went back to the centre of this village, we came upon a scene. There was one soldier wearing a fur hat stepping on another man's, another soldier's head, squashing it. We believed that the man underneath was probably a Croatian prisoner and that the other man was trying to crunch his head. We came closer to see exactly what was going on and the nose of the man who was underneath was bleeding, blood pouring on to the floor. It was a grotesque situation because they had quarrelled about a car and the other plan was trying to squash his head so that he could have the other man's car. One of those who were with me said, "It's totally pointless for you to come to blows over a car." Borovo Naselje was teeming with these paramilitary units, Territorial Defence detachments, local units. The reason, I understood at the time, was that there were many things to be looted there so they had really come into their own, you might say, in Borovo Naselje. They had all those yellow boots, displaying them as war trophies. Borovo Selo had a factory which produced these yellow boots that were fashionable at the time so they were carrying them around as trophies, tied around their necks. And all sorts of different things but these yellow boots are something that I remember in a particularly vivid way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. You just mentioned that there were paramilitary units and Territorial Defence. In what way can you identify the soldiers as belonging to those kind of units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't a problem because I had rich experience on that score. That was the least of my problems, to be able to recognise a regular soldier and differentiate between them and paramilitaries. With the proviso that this did not mean that the conduct of a regular soldier and that of a paramilitary was the same or was not the same. You had to be very careful in your definitions. So both would be prone to get drunk and loot, but the others were marked because the two that quarrelled over the golf car belonged to a unit called the White Eagles. Now, whether they actually were members of that unit, you couldn't really tell because sometimes they would just brag and a few of them would get together and say, "Now we are going to war" and they would give each other names or their groups names, but they did recognise each other and you could also distinguish between paramilitaries and the others, if you had enough experience. You could identify who was who, judging by their outward appearance, their physical appearance. They usually had caps with cockades, beards, various insignia on them, and even different kinds of emblems and we could even define which party they belonged to. They talked a lot. So it wasn't difficult to gain that information because in the Balkans we are prone to be gregarious and talk a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a small intervention with respect to the interpretation. When the witness was talking, he was describing a vehicle that is -- was the Golf vehicle. On page 63 in the translation, it says "golf car." Not to be confused with the game golf and a golf car for the golf game.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. I can see where your mind is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I would like to turn up a map, because the witness had been talking about the -- describing the village Borovo Naselje. And that is the ERN number 04626621. And that is map number 5 in the compilation. I also would like to take the opportunity to ask to tender that into evidence because, according to my information, it has not have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think you can take it that the Chamber knows the location on the map.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you just want to tender it we can do that and move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think Defence counsel know it as well. That map will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 115, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Well, we didn't stay there long because my colleague wanted to see Vukovar, but from the other side. So that we went back because he had some of his own assignments that he had to see to and it suited me, too, because I had an assignment too. I had something to do in the old part of Vukovar, in the other part.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: What kind of assignment was that? Can you describe what it was and what you did observe in that -- during that assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: May we close -- go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I finished my conversation with this man, and we promised to meet under more normal circumstances and we would be able to talk about things in a different way, that's how we parted. I returned to the old part of town, of Vukovar, as I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: After that, did you meet any person? And in that sense, can you tell us what you saw or were told?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: What I'm going to talk about now is to my mind very important but requires protective measures, this encounter with this friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: May I ask the witness if the witness then intends to mention a name that could be linked to the witness's identity? Is it so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Not only the name, but also an explanation which is directly linked to my own person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Can the witness if there were any specific incident when you were together with this person that we have been talking about and describe us what that was in the sense -- in that sense. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm following you. Could you explain the question? I'm a little tired already so perhaps I wasn't following.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did this person describe another fighter or soldier and what that person then were doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I don't know. Apart from that conversation there on that spot, nothing else happened, as far as I recall --

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: -- before we set off to another location.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'll return back to the person we were talking about. Did he say anything about war booty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Ah, well, that happened when we -- or rather when I went off with that acquaintance of mine. We spent some time in the company of his fellow fighters, and then we went off to a house where a unit had its headquarters. I didn't know who made up those units, which participated in the Vukovar operations, so I wasn't really interested. I didn't have to know that, wasn't required to. But it was a Lieutenant Colonel. I assume he was the Chief of Staff of some group or other. He was certainly not a commander. And he was very unpleasant when he greeted me. He almost swore at me. And started saying that everything that was happening was not being portrayed in the proper way, that he had lost many young men and that they would be soon forgotten. And he was really furious. He was furious at the Supreme Command, which had not managed the Vukovar operation properly. And he was angry first and foremost at those who had allowed the paramilitary units to take part in the battle for Vukovar. And then he told me -- well, I could say he described a comical scene. This is what he said. He received an order to hand over two APCs to the Serbian Volunteer Guard, Arkan's men, because there were a lot of wounded. He sent off two APCs but, according to his words, he kept thinking about those APCs and they kept moving around in the area next to his headquarters where he was stationed, and the headquarters were right up along the road. He said he would leave the building, leave the cellar, and he stopped the APC on one occasion. He asked the driver what all that was about. And the driver kept quiet. He ordered him to open up the APC, and he found a full load of television sets, white goods, and everything else, tape recorders, and a whole manner of household devices, appliances. He called the soldiers and they threw everything out into the ditch. He did the same thing with the second APC, which was also full of household appliances. And what happened next? An hour later, his commander, the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, called him up, General Andrija Biorcevic was his name, and told him that he must not destroy any more war booty. Now, he asked me whether I was aware of the fact that televisions and tape recorders and household appliances were actually war booty, would I agree with that. I was dumb-founded, and that's what happened at that command post.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. And this was the 19th of November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Yes. That was the 19th, the next day.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: And the next day, the 20th, were you then in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I was not in Vukovar. I was at about 30 to 40 kilometres away from Vukovar in another locality.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at any point of time after your presence in Vukovar talk with someone about Vukovar in a specific sense?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Yes. I did have occasion to do that. And it was towards the end of November 1992. I know that for certain because on the 28th of November of that year I had returned from spending a month in another locality. It was a chance encounter in town, and the man in question was a member of the unit which I mentioned a moment ago. Or, rather, he was from the same unit that that other young man was from, the one driving the motor, except that this one was an officer. And according to my information, he was the most capable of them all, of all the members of that unit. And he had the command responsibility of -- he had a command responsibility but I'm not sure whether he was the commander of the unit or not. He might have been. He wasn't a Serb or Montenegrin by ethnicity, and he complained to me that he had been transferred from the operative unit to an office. I can only imagine how the man must have felt, because at that time, when I knew them, their job was just training, to be trained as well as possible and capacitated for the assignments they were to carry out. We stood out in the street and talked. We were standing to one side so nobody could overhear our conversation. I realised that he was very affected. I couldn't understand him properly at the time but I eventually understood what he had meant when the same thing happened to me two months later. This was the 28th of November 1992 and the same thing happened to me on the 23rd of February 1993, not even a full two months later. Was he bitter? I assume that he was but he would not have told me what he told me had the situation been normal. He said, "They divvied out all the ranks and decorations to Vukovar's heroes," and roughly speaking he said, "Look what happened to me." And he told me how Mrksic and Sljivancanin got all the glory to themselves. He told me about valuable things that were taken from the Eltz castle. He talked about money that had been taken. He said, "Vukovar's truth will never be known. And I mean the dark aspect of the whole story." At one point, he said, "Mrksic and Sljivancanin ordered for those people from the hospital to be killed." I'm standing there looking at him, unable to believe what he was saying. I didn't have the information myself, not at all. And I believe I wouldn't be too far wrong if I say that I was quite well-informed. I saw those people alive. So I asked this gentleman to provide more detail, to tell me how it was and what exactly happened. Roughly speaking, he tells me this: "Sljivancanin and Radic picked soldiers, officers and NCOs that they trusted, they secured the spot." He said that the people from the hospital had been killed in a waste spot, in a spot of waste land. I remember that he used the term "waste land," which struck me as peculiar, but it wasn't until many years later that people started talking about a place called Ovcara and so on and so forth. Truth to tell, I wasn't exactly glad that he told me what he told me. At the time, the best thing was to know as least as possible. You were better off and a lot safer that way. At least that's how I was reasoning at the time. I'm not sure where he lives now or what he's doing. All my contacts broke off, as it were, back in 1993, and personally I was no longer interested in people or events from that time of my life.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Did this officer mentioned who executed or who did do the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a little the worse for wear and my focus is not what it used to be but he said those people were executed by members of the Territorial Defence unit, the one that I saw on the ground there, and the paramilitaries. The crime screen was secured by regular JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name of there officer? And before -- if you do know that, then you will ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-016
utterances.text: I did know it for a while but, as I said, he was not a Serb or Montenegrin by ethnicity so that's the extent of what I know about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: My examination-in-chief is done, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've well and truly run over time so we now must adjourn. We will resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.07 p.m., to
